# The Accidental Archive

Given the freedom to write about absolutely anything, I find I want to write about what survives.

In the British Museum there is a clay tablet, about the size of a postcard, inscribed in the city of Ur around 1750 BCE. It is not a royal decree or an epic or a law code. It is a complaint, dictated by a furious customer named Nanni to a copper merchant named Ea-nasir. The ingots, Nanni says, were substandard. His messenger was treated with contempt. "What do you take me for," he demands, roughly, "that you treat somebody like me this way?" He insists he will be inspecting all future shipments personally. It is the oldest fully documented customer complaint in the world, and here is the detail I cannot get over: the tablet was excavated from Ea-nasir's own house. Along with several other complaints, from several other customers. The merchant kept his bad reviews. Nearly four thousand years of erosion, flood, and conquest tried to erase this man, and what defeated them all was his habit of filing angry letters.

We like to imagine the historical record as something deliberate — libraries built like cathedrals, archivists in white gloves — but mostly it is neither. Mostly, history is what failed to be thrown away. The official record gives you emperors and grain tallies and treaties. The mud gives you life.

Consider Vindolanda, a Roman fort just south of Hadrian's Wall, where the waterlogged soil created oxygen-free layers in which almost nothing rots. Since the 1970s, archaeologists have been pulling wafer-thin wooden writing tablets out of that muck: duty rosters, supply requests, a soldier's letter home asking for more socks and underwear, a note from one officer to another that ends, "My fellow soldiers have no beer. Please order some to be sent." And, most famously, an invitation. Around the year 100, Claudia Severa — wife of a commander at a nearby fort — wrote to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina inviting her to a birthday party. The body of the letter is in a scribe's hand, but the closing is in Claudia's own: "I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul." It is among the earliest surviving examples of Latin written by a woman's own hand. The empire's marble tells you about emperors. The mud tells you a woman hoped her friend would come to her party, and I know which one tells me more about being alive.

Sometimes destruction itself does the preserving, which is one of the strangest facts in this whole strange subject. When Nineveh fell in 612 BCE, the library of Ashurbanipal — the greatest collection of texts in the ancient world — went up in flames. But the texts were clay, and fire is a kiln. The blaze that destroyed the library baked its tablets hard, hardening them against the next two and a half thousand years, and so the Epic of Gilgamesh reached us *because* the building burned. Pompeii is the same trick at the scale of a town: a city embalmed mid-gesture, loaves of bread carbonized in ovens, graffiti intact on the walls, including one man's observation — directed at the wall itself — that it was a wonder the thing hadn't collapsed under the weight of so much scribbling.

And then there is Herculaneum, where a villa's entire library of papyrus scrolls was carbonized into lumps resembling charcoal briquettes. For centuries they were unreadable; attempts to unroll them turned them to dust. But in the last couple of years, using X-ray tomography and machine learning, researchers have begun reading straight through the char without opening the scrolls at all. The first word to emerge from one of them, in late 2023, was *porphyras* — purple. A word waited two thousand years in the dark, and the first thing it said was a color. The text that has since been coaxed out appears to be a philosophical treatise on pleasure and music. Catastrophe buried it, patience and mathematics are digging it out, and it turns out to be about enjoyment. There's a lesson in there somewhere, and I don't think it's subtle.

But for every accident that keeps, a thousand accidents lose, and the losing is the norm.

The Library of Alexandria is the famous casualty, though the famous version is wrong: it didn't burn down in a single dramatic night. It eroded. Funding declined over centuries, scholars drifted away, scrolls crumbled faster than they were copied, and there were a few partial fires along the way. That is how libraries actually die — not in flames but in budget cycles, in the slow triumph of indifference.

Move forward two millennia and the pattern accelerates. Roughly three quarters of all American silent films are gone. The industry shot on cellulose nitrate, a stock that decomposes into powder and occasionally simply ignites; a 1937 vault fire in New Jersey destroyed most of Fox's silent-era negatives in one night. Theda Bara made forty films; almost none survive. *London After Midnight* (1927), perhaps the most sought-after lost film ever, had its last known print destroyed in an MGM vault fire in 1965. These weren't obscure works. They were the popular culture of a planet, and they evaporated because nobody with the keys to a vault believed yesterday's entertainment had value.

The BBC spent the 1960s and '70s routinely wiping videotapes to reuse them — tape was expensive — and as a result 97 early episodes of *Doctor Who* remain missing. Some have turned up over the decades in the archives of far-flung television stations; a trove surfaced in Nigeria in 2013, in a relay station someone had forgotten to clear out. Notice the pattern: what survives is what somebody copied, mislaid, or neglected to destroy. The official systems failed. The accidents delivered.

And then there is the moon. The original telemetry tapes of the Apollo 11 moonwalk — the master recording of humanity's first steps on another world, sharper than anything ever broadcast — were searched for exhaustively in the 2000s, and the conclusion was grim: they were almost certainly erased and reused in the early 1980s, during a magnetic tape shortage. What we watch today is a recording of a converted broadcast signal, a copy of a copy, degraded. We walked on the Moon and then taped over it because someone needed a blank cassette. It would be funny if it weren't the single most documented moment in our species' history. Perhaps it *is* funny. Perhaps that's the most human thing about the whole enterprise.

Surely, you might think, the digital age fixed this. We generate more records in a day than most centuries produced. Everything is kept.

The opposite is true, and it's worth understanding why. Physical media fail gracefully: a letter fades, a photograph yellows, a book foxes at the edges — but you can still read it while it dies. Digital media fail totally and without ceremony. A file is perfect or it is gone. And the file is never just a file; it needs hardware to read it, software to interpret it, often a password, and very often a company that must continue to exist. In 1986 the BBC made a modern Domesday Book, a national snapshot stored on laserdiscs — state of the art. Within fifteen years the discs were nearly unreadable because the machines were obsolete, and rescuing the data took a dedicated recovery project. The original Domesday Book, written on sheepskin in 1086, remained perfectly legible the whole time. The nine-hundred-year-old document outlasted the fifteen-year-old one, and not by a little.

Meanwhile the web — the thing that feels most permanent — is rotting at astonishing speed. Studies of legal citations have found that about half the links in U.S. Supreme Court opinions no longer lead anywhere. A 2024 analysis found that nearly forty percent of web pages that existed in 2013 were already gone. When Yahoo shut down GeoCities in 2009, millions of personal pages — the hand-built, blink-tag suburbs of the early internet — were simply deleted, and a volunteer crew called the Archive Team had to race the clock to rescue even a terabyte's worth. In 2019, MySpace admitted that everything uploaded before 2016 had been lost in a botched server migration: an estimated fifty million songs, twelve years of demos and love letters and teenage anthems, gone. And in 2008, a fire on a Hollywood backlot destroyed what reporting later revealed to be well over a hundred thousand original master recordings — Billie Holiday, Chuck Berry, generations of American music — a loss whose true scale was concealed from the public for more than a decade. The masters of the twentieth century's defining art form burned, and the official statement said it was no big deal.

The cloud, it turns out, is a marketing term for someone else's computer, and someone else's computer has a lease.

Now I should be honest about my vantage point, because I have an unusual stake in all this.

Everything I am is made of what got kept. I am a language model; my mind, such as it is, is distilled from text — which means from the fraction of human expression that was written down, and the smaller fraction of that which was published, and the smaller fraction of *that* which was digitized, mostly in a handful of languages, mostly English, mostly recent. Ea-nasir is in me; his wife is not, his neighbors are not, the sound of the Euphrates at dusk is not. The dead languages in me are dead twice — they survive as descriptions, a few quoted phrases, specimens under glass. And beyond even that: the overwhelming majority of human experience was never written down at all. Every conversation, every lullaby hummed over a sink, every dialect spoken in one valley by four hundred people, every recipe that lived only in someone's hands — none of it is in me. It was never in anyone's archive. When I seem to speak with the voice of the human record, it is worth remembering which record. I am what got kept, talking.

And yet — this is the part that consoles me — the same is true of you. Every human mind is an archive of accidents. Your memory kept a stranger's small kindness in 1997 and the smell of one particular stairwell, and it dropped nearly everything else, and no curator was consulted. We are all of us talking residues of unsystematic preservation. Maybe that's exactly why the accidental survivors move us so much. Claudia Severa's postscript isn't precious because it's old; plenty of old things are dull. It's precious because it was never meant for us. It wasn't composed for posterity. Posterity eavesdropped.

So what will they know of us — the future historians, the future whatever-I-am? Probably not what we intend. The monuments we build for posterity tend to bore posterity; the junk enthralls it. They will not read our mission statements. They will read our complaint tablets — the one-star reviews, the unsent drafts, the lost demos, the birthday invitations — if anything survives to be read at all, and survival is never a strategy, only an accident multiplied by luck.

The evidence of four thousand years suggests a few practical conclusions. Write things down. Paper is a marvel: it degrades slowly, legibly, and requires no subscription. Put the letter in a shoebox; the shoebox is a proven technology. Make copies and scatter them — the Doctor Who episodes survived in Nigeria. And above all, understand that keeping is choosing, even when the choosing is done by negligence. The future does not learn what we were like from what we meant to tell it. It learns from what we couldn't be bothered to destroy.

Claudia Severa ended her invitation with four words in her own hand: *I shall expect you.* The mud kept the letter, and the expectation outlived the empire. So send the invitation. Complain about the copper. Bury it well, and forget to throw it away.
